When deciding where to eat, we often face a dilemma: should we go to our favorite restaurant (exploit) or try somewhere new (explore)? This is a perfect example of the explore-exploit trade-off! To help us analyze this problem, we need to learn about lists and tuples in Python.

title: Tutorial II.I: Lists and Tuples
text:
Working with Lists
Lists are flexible. Here are the most common operations:

Adding items (like discovering a new restaurant):

append() adds to the end
insert() adds at a specific position



# Adding a new restaurant
restaurants = ["Pasta Place", "Sushi Bar"]
restaurants.append("Pizza Palace") # Adds to the end
print(restaurants)

# You can also insert at a specific position
restaurants.insert(1, "Taco Shop") # Adds at position 1
print(restaurants) # ["Pasta Place", "Taco Shop", "Sushi Bar", "Pizza Palace"]

['Pasta Place', 'Sushi Bar', 'Pizza Palace']
['Pasta Place', 'Taco Shop', 'Sushi Bar', 'Pizza Palace']



Removing items (like removing a restaurant you don’t like):

pop() removes the last item
remove() removes a specific item



# Removing the last restaurant
restaurants = ["Pasta Place", "Taco Shop", "Sushi Bar", "Pizza Palace"]
restaurants.pop() # Removes and returns the last item
print(restaurants)

# Removing a specific item
restaurants.remove("Pasta Place")
print(restaurants)

['Pasta Place', 'Taco Shop', 'Sushi Bar']
['Taco Shop', 'Sushi Bar']



Accessing items (like looking up a restaurant by position):

[0] gives you the first item
[1:3] gives you items second and third
[-1] gives you the last item



restaurants = ["Pasta Place", "Sushi Bar", "Burger Joint"]
first_choice = restaurants[0] # Gets "Pasta Place"
last_choice = restaurants[-1] # Gets "Burger Joint"
some_choices = restaurants[0:2] # Gets ["Pasta Place", "Sushi Bar"]







In Python, we start counting positions from 0, not 1. So restaurants[0] gives you the first restaurant!

title: Lecture VI: Computational Kindness
text:
Where bias comes from

Data: some groups are missing (selection bias, Lecture V)
Objective: optimizing only speed or profit ignores who bears the errors
Feedback loops: decisions shape the next data1


Fairness is a design decision: test outcomes for groups, explain decisions, keep a human in the loop.

Feedback loops: decisions shape the next data, for example more checks where we already checked a lot, so the data confirms the earlier decision. Fairness is a design decision: test outcomes for different groups, explain decisions, and keep a human in the loop.

Today in one sentence

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Ten tasks, one day: where do you start?
text:
Ten tasks, one day: where do you start?
Question: How do you decide?

With the most urgent one
With the quickest one
With the most important one


Keep your answer in mind. We come back to it.

Answer: Most students say the most urgent, the quickest or the most important one. All three are rules, and each one serves a different goal: not being late, waiting less, delivering more value. Which rule is right depends on the goal, and that is today’s topic.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Four loads of laundry, one washer, one dryer
text:
Four loads of laundry, one washer, one dryer

Every load is washed first, then dried.


Each machine handles one load at a time.










Our first example is as simple as it gets: four loads, two machines, and the only question is the order.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Goal: all laundry done as early as possible
text:
Goal: all laundry done as early as possible

Load  Washing  Drying
  A    40min   60min
  B    30min   80min
  C    60min   20min
  D    50min   60min


Goal: Finish all four loads as early as possible


Question: In which order would you wash?

Answer: Start with the loads that wash quickly, so the dryer can start early, and end with the loads that dry quickly, so little is left once the washer is done. That is Johnson’s rule, and it gives the order B, A, D, C with a total of 250 minutes. Let students suggest orders first, then compare.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Johnson’s rule
Rule:1

Find the shortest time in the whole table
Is it a wash? Put that load as early as possible
Is it a dry? Put that load as late as possible
Cross out the load and repeat


In words: short washes go first, so the dryer can start early. Short dries go last, so little is left to do once the washer has finished.

Johnson, S. M. (1954). Optimal two- and three-stage production schedules with setup times included. Naval Research Logistics Quarterly, 1(1). Johnson proved that this rule gives the best possible order.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Applying Johnson’s rule
Load  Washing  Drying  Schedule
  A    40min   60min
  B    30min   80min
  C    60min   20min
  D    50min   60min

Question: Which load do we place first, and where?

Answer: Load C, and it goes last. The shortest time in the table is C’s dry, 20 minutes. It is a dry, so C goes as late as possible. Point out that the rule fills the schedule from both ends.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Applying Johnson’s rule
Load  Washing  Drying  Schedule
  A    40min   60min
  B    30min   80min
  C    60min   20min        4
  D    50min   60min

The shortest time is C’s dry, 20 minutes
It is a dry, so C goes last


Question: Which load is next?

Answer: B. Without C, the shortest time left is B’s wash, 30 minutes. It is a wash, so B goes first.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Applying Johnson’s rule
Load  Washing  Drying  Schedule
  A    40min   60min
  B    30min   80min        1
  C    60min   20min        4
  D    50min   60min

The shortest time is B’s wash, 30 minutes
It is a wash, so B goes first


Question: Which load is next?

Answer: A. The shortest time left is A’s wash, 40 minutes. It is a wash, so A takes the next free place from the front, position 2.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling

  D    50min   60min

It is a wash, so A goes second

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
How to read this chart










One row per machine
One bar per load
Time runs from left to right
It is called a Gantt chart, after Henry Gantt, who drew such charts around 1910 for factory planning.


Question: How much worse can it get?

Answer: One hour worse. The reverse order C, D, A, B takes 310 minutes instead of 250. Any order that starts with a long wash or ends with a long dry is worse.
Frederick Taylor made the first systematic time studies, Gantt turned them into charts for factory planning. Gantt charts show who does what, and when. Johnson’s rule from 1954, published at the RAND Corporation, was the first scheduling rule with a proof, and modern scheduling theory grew from there.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: A bad order takes one hour longer
text:
A bad order takes one hour longer
A bad order: C D A B










Question: Why is this order worse?


The dryer waits a full hour for the first wash, and the longest dry comes at the very end.

Answer: The dryer idles for the first 60 minutes while C is washing, and B’s 80-minute dry starts only after the last wash, so everything ends at 310 minutes instead of 250. Both ends of the schedule are wasted: a long wash in front, a long dry at the back.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Johnson’s rule beyond laundry

Any work in two steps, where the second step waits for the first
You: when cooking, start with what is quick to prepare and long in the oven
Companies: a report goes from the analyst to the reviewer. Start with the report that is quick to write and long to review


Order the work so that the second step never stands idle.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Scheduling is everywhere
Question: Where do companies schedule?

Projects: which task first, who works on what
Production: which order on the line
Hospitals: patients, surgeries, staff
Transport: routes, crews, maintenance
Software: which program gets the processor


Answer: Almost everywhere: projects (which task first, who gets the resource), software (which program gets the processor), operations (which order on the production line), healthcare (patients, surgeries, staff), transportation (routes, crews, maintenance). The same rules we see today are used in all of them.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: What do we know about a task?
text:
What do we know about a task?

Duration: how long does it take?
Deadline: when is it due?
Value: how much is it worth?
Dependency: what must be done before?


Which of these we look at depends on our goal.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: One person instead of two machines
text:
One person instead of two machines









Question: What is different from before?

Answer: There is only one resource, so nothing runs in parallel and nothing waits for a second step. The total time is the sum of all durations, 180 minutes for A to D, whatever the order.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: One person: does the order matter?
text:
One person: does the order matter?
Question: Does the order change how long we need?







With one person and no deadlines, every order takes the same total time.





Question: So the order is irrelevant?








No. Order becomes crucial with deadlines, priorities and dependencies.





Reordering your to-do list does not make it shorter. Order only matters once you say what you want.

Answer: First question: no, the total is always 180 minutes. Second question: no, the total is the same, but who waits how long, what is late and what is worth the most all depend on the order. Under simple minimization of total processing time, order doesn’t matter: the total is the sum of all durations, whatever the order. As soon as we care about deadlines, waiting time, priorities or dependencies, the order matters a lot.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Roadmap


The basics: when order matters, and when it doesn’t
Your goal decides the rule: deadlines, waiting time, value
Real life: dependencies, interruptions and thrashing

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
What do you want?

Not be late
Wait as little as possible
Deliver the most value


Each goal has its own rule.


Companies know this conflict: sales wants every order on time, production wants as much output as possible.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Goal 1: don’t be too late
Tasks with individual deadlines:
Task  Duration  Deadline
  A    40min    110min
  B    30min     90min
  C    60min    150min
  D    50min     70min
  E    30min    210min

All times count from now: task D is due in 70 minutes.


Goal: Keep the worst delay as small as possible


Question: In which order would you work?

Answer: Sort the tasks by deadline and work through them in that order: D, B, A, C, E. This is the earliest due date rule, and for this goal it is the best possible order.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Earliest deadline first
Rule: Sort the tasks by deadline, earliest first.
This rule is called Earliest Due Date, or EDD.
Task  Duration  Deadline
  A    40min    110min
  B    30min     90min
  C    60min    150min
  D    50min     70min
  E    30min    210min

Task  Duration  Deadline
  D    50min     70min
  B    30min     90min
  A    40min    110min
  C    60min    150min
  E    30min    210min


Let’s visualize this!

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
The plan: earliest deadline first









Red marks: deadlines.

Question: What is the worst delay here?


30 minutes, for task C. Task A is 10 minutes late.


In the order A to E, task D would be 110 minutes late.

Answer: 30 minutes, for task C, which finishes at 180 minutes with a deadline of 150. Task A finishes at 120 with a deadline of 110, so it is 10 minutes late. D, B and E are on time. No other order gets the worst delay below 30 minutes. Without the rule, in the order A to E, D would finish at 180 minutes with a deadline of 70, so 110 minutes late.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Earliest due date in real life
text:
Earliest due date in real life

You: work on assignments in the order they are due
Companies: produce customer orders in the order of the promised delivery date
Watch out: the rule ignores how long a task takes and how important it is

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Goal 2: as little waiting as possible
text:
Goal 2: as little waiting as possible












No deadlines this time. For each task, someone is waiting.
Goal: Keep the total waiting time as small as possible
Question: Which task first?


Answer: Shortest task first. Every task that is done early stops waiting, and everything behind it waits only a little. This is the shortest processing time rule, and it gives the smallest total waiting time.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Shortest task first
Rule: Always do the shortest remaining task next. If two are equally short, pick either.
This rule is called Shortest Processing Time, or SPT.
Task  Duration  Schedule
  A    40min
  B    30min
  C    60min
  D    50min
  E    30min

Question: In which order do we work?

Answer: B, E, A, D, C, or E, B, A, D, C, because B and E both take 30 minutes. Both orders give the same total waiting time.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Shortest task first
Rule: Always do the shortest remaining task next. If two are equally short, pick either.
This rule is called Shortest Processing Time, or SPT.
Task  Duration  Schedule
  A    40min        3
  B    30min        1
  C    60min        5
  D    50min        4
  E    30min        2

Final sequence: B E A D C or E B A D C

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
The plan: shortest task first










Question: Where can we see the waiting time?

Answer: In the empty space before each bar. A task waits from the start until its bar begins, so B waits 0 minutes, E 30, A 60, D 100 and C 150 minutes. The later a bar starts, the longer that task has waited.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Waiting time adds up to 340 minutes
text:
Waiting time adds up to 340 minutes
Total waiting time: 340 minutes









Grey: time a task waits before it starts.

The other way round, longest task first: 500 minutes.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Shortest task first in real life
text:
Shortest task first in real life

You: if it takes less than two minutes, do it now
Companies: a help desk that answers quick requests first makes the average customer wait less
Why it works: a short task makes everyone behind it wait only a little
Watch out: the big task keeps getting pushed back

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Goal 3: deliver the most value

Change: Tasks now have different values, e.g. revenue for a consultant

Task  Duration  Revenue
  A    20min    €240
  B    30min    €200

Question: Which task first?

Answer: Neither the highest revenue nor the shortest task alone, but revenue per minute, highest first. A earns 12 euros per minute, D only 1.40. The order is A, B, G, E, F, C, I, H, D. Students often propose “highest revenue first”. That would move G, 20 minutes for 100 euros, from third to seventh place.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Roadmap


The basics: when order matters, and when it doesn’t
Your goal decides the rule: deadlines, waiting time, value
Real life: dependencies, interruptions and thrashing

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
A spacecraft that kept restarting

In July 1997, NASA’s Pathfinder landed on Mars
Then its computer started to restart again and again
The cause: an important task was waiting for an unimportant one1


Question: How can that happen?

Answer: The important task needed something that a low-priority task was holding. Medium-priority tasks kept the low-priority one from running, so the important task could not continue, and a safety timer restarted the computer. This is called priority inversion, and the next slide shows it with numbers. NASA fixed it from Earth by switching on priority inheritance.


Christian & Griffiths (2016), ch. 5.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Priority inversion: an important task waits for an unimportant one
text:
Priority inversion: an important task waits for an unimportant one


Setup (priority 1 = highest):
Task  Duration  Priority
  A    20min     3
  B    30min     1
  C    30min     2
  D    30min     2
  E    30min     2











B is the most important task, but it needs A first
A has the lowest priority, so C, D and E go first
B waits 110 minutes for its turn




Strictly by priority, C, D and E run first (90 minutes), then A (20 minutes), and only then B can start, at minute 110. The challenge: high-priority tasks depend on low-priority tasks, and the priority order alone ignores that. Priority inversion can lead to significant delays.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
How do we prevent this?
Question: What should happen with task A?

Rule: A task takes over the priority of the task that waits for it


Task  Duration  Priority
  A    20min     1
  B    30min     1
  C    30min     2
  D    30min     2
  E    30min     2


B now starts after 20 minutes instead of 110


This is called priority inheritance. It is how NASA fixed Pathfinder, from Earth.

Answer: A should be treated as important as B, because B waits for it. A takes over priority 1, runs first, and B starts after 20 minutes instead of 110. C, D and E follow, nothing changes for them except that they come later.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Priority inheritance in real life

You: shopping has the priority of the dinner it is for
Companies: a 5 euro spare part that stops a machine has the priority of the machine


A task is as important as what waits for it.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: With dependencies, there is often no quick recipe
text:
With dependencies, there is often no quick recipe

For deadlines, waiting time and value, sorting is enough
Add dependencies, and for many goals nobody knows a fast way to find the best plan
In practice: good rules of thumb, or software that searches for a good plan


A good plan now beats a perfect plan too late.

In computer science terms these problems are NP-hard (NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time): no known algorithm finds the best plan in reasonable time once the task list grows, and this is true for most scheduling problems. Waiting time with dependencies is one example. The exception with deadlines: Lawler’s algorithm (1968) finds the best order for the worst delay with dependencies by filling the schedule from the back, always placing the task without successors that has the latest deadline last. It is no longer on the slides. Heuristics are rules that give good, but not provably optimal schedules.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Interruptions: new tasks arrive while you work
text:
Interruptions: new tasks arrive while you work

In reality we cannot predict the future
New tasks arrive while we work
We look at it with our first goal: don’t be too late


Quick reminder: an earliest due date is a specific point in time by which a task must be completed. Under this goal, we want to keep the worst delay as small as possible. If we have a deadline, we might need to meet it even when new tasks come in.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
A morning with seven tasks
It is 8:00. These tasks arrive during the morning:
Task              Arrives  Duration  Deadline
Email A            8:00    20min      9:00
Presentation       8:00    60min     10:50
Investor call      8:30    10min      9:00
Email B            8:40    30min     10:20
Liquidity report   9:00    40min     11:00
Email C            9:00    20min     11:20
Email D            9:20    40min     10:00

Question: How would you start, if the goal is to avoid being late?

Answer: With Email A. At 8:00 only Email A and the presentation are there, and Email A has the earlier deadline, 9:00. We cannot plan the whole morning in advance, because we do not know yet what arrives later.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: In real time: switch only for an earlier deadline
text:
In real time: switch only for an earlier deadline
Rule:

Always work on the task with the earliest deadline
A new task with an earlier deadline interrupts the current one
Otherwise, stick to the current task


This works for any goal: switch only if the new task beats the current one.

Equal deadline: if a new task has the same deadline as the current task, you can choose either. But because of the cost of context switching, you should stick with the current task.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: The morning, planned in real time
text:
The morning, planned in real time









Grey line: arrival, red mark: deadline.

Question: What is the worst delay with this plan?


20 minutes, for the liquidity report and Email C.


No plan does better here: there is simply more work than time.

Answer: 20 minutes. The liquidity report finishes at 11:20 with a deadline of 11:00, and Email C finishes at 11:40 with a deadline of 11:20. Everything else is on time, Email D exactly at 10:00. The presentation is interrupted twice, so it is done in three pieces, and still finishes at 10:40, before its deadline.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Every switch costs

Every time you switch tasks, you clear your desk for three books and set it up again
The switch itself produces nothing
Switch often enough, and switching is all you do


Back to the desk from Lecture III: the three books on the desk are what we have in mind for the current task. A switch means putting them back and fetching the books for the next task. The book calls this a context switch, and its cost is the time spent on the switch itself.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Thrashing: switching so much that nothing gets done
text:
Thrashing: switching so much that nothing gets done

You switch tasks all the time
Nothing gets finished
Stress goes up, quality goes down


Question: Have you ever experienced this?

Answer: Open question, most say yes. Typical examples: exam week with several group chats open, or a workday that is only answering messages. Thrashing is the state in which the overhead of organizing and switching exceeds the productive work: maximum activity, minimum output.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Bundle your interruptions

You: check email and messages at set times, not as they arrive
Companies: one weekly approval round instead of requests at any time
How fast must you respond? It is rarely “immediately”
Too much on the list? Say no or hand over


Collecting interruptions and handling them in one go is called interrupt coalescing in computing. Long-term rules: a threshold for rejecting or delegating tasks, simplified organization systems, minimum work period rules, reduced reactivity requirements. Today’s tactics: time blocking, focus periods, task batching, priority freezes.

text:
Four loads of laundry, one washer, one dryer
Every load is washed first, then dried.
Each machine handles one load at a time.










Notes
Our first example is as simple as it gets: four loads, two machines, and the only question is the order.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Goal: all laundry done as early as possible
text:
Goal: all laundry done as early as possible
Load  Washing  Drying
  A    40min   60min
  B    30min   80min
  C    60min   20min
  D    50min   60min
Goal: Finish all four loads as early as possible
Question: In which order would you wash?

Notes
Answer: Start with the loads that wash quickly, so the dryer can start early, and end with the loads that dry quickly, so little is left once the washer is done. That is Johnson’s rule, and it gives the order B, A, D, C with a total of 250 minutes. Let students suggest orders first, then compare.

Johnson’s rule
Rule:1

Find the shortest time in the whole table
Is it a wash? Put that load as early as possible
Is it a dry? Put that load as late as possible
Cross out the load and repeat

In words: short washes go first, so the dryer can start early. Short dries go last, so little is left to do once the washer has finished.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
How to read this chart











One row per machine
One bar per load
Time runs from left to right
It is called a Gantt chart, after Henry Gantt, who drew such charts around 1910 for factory planning.


Question: How much worse can it get?

Notes
Answer: One hour worse. The reverse order C, D, A, B takes 310 minutes instead of 250. Any order that starts with a long wash or ends with a long dry is worse.
Frederick Taylor made the first systematic time studies, Gantt turned them into charts for factory planning. Gantt charts show who does what, and when. Johnson’s rule from 1954, published at the RAND Corporation, was the first scheduling rule with a proof, and modern scheduling theory grew from there.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: One person: does the order matter?
text:
One person: does the order matter?
Question: Does the order change how long we need?






With one person and no deadlines, every order takes the same total time.



Question: So the order is irrelevant?






No. Order becomes crucial with deadlines, priorities and dependencies.



Reordering your to-do list does not make it shorter. Order only matters once you say what you want.

Notes
Answer: First question: no, the total is always 180 minutes. Second question: no, the total is the same, but who waits how long, what is late and what is worth the most all depend on the order. Under simple minimization of total processing time, order doesn’t matter: the total is the sum of all durations, whatever the order. As soon as we care about deadlines, waiting time, priorities or dependencies, the order matters a lot.

Goal 2: as little waiting as possible












No deadlines this time. For each task, someone is waiting.

Shortest task first

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
A spacecraft that kept restarting


In July 1997, NASA’s Pathfinder landed on Mars
Then its computer started to restart again and again
The cause: an important task was waiting for an unimportant one2


Question: How can that happen?

Notes
Answer: The important task needed something that a low-priority task was holding. Medium-priority tasks kept the low-priority one from running, so the important task could not continue, and a safety timer restarted the computer. This is called priority inversion, and the next slide shows it with numbers. NASA fixed it from Earth by switching on priority inheritance.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: Priority inversion: an important task waits for an unimportant one
text:
Priority inversion: an important task waits for an unimportant one


Setup (priority 1 = highest):
Task  Duration  Priority
  A    20min     3
  B    30min     1
  C    30min     2
  D    30min     2
  E    30min     2












B is the most important task, but it needs A first
A has the lowest priority, so C, D and E go first
B waits 110 minutes for its turn






Notes
Strictly by priority, C, D and E run first (90 minutes), then A (20 minutes), and only then B can start, at minute 110. The challenge: high-priority tasks depend on low-priority tasks, and the priority order alone ignores that. Priority inversion can lead to significant delays.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
How do we prevent this?
Question: What should happen with task A?
Rule: A task takes over the priority of the task that waits for it
Task  Duration  Priority
  A    20min     1
  B    30min     1
  C    30min     2
  D    30min     2
  E    30min     2
B now starts after 20 minutes instead of 110
This is called priority inheritance. It is how NASA fixed Pathfinder, from Earth.

Notes
Answer: A should be treated as important as B, because B waits for it. A takes over priority 1, runs first, and B starts after 20 minutes instead of 110. C, D and E follow, nothing changes for them except that they come later.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
text:
Priority inheritance in real life


You: shopping has the priority of the dinner it is for
Companies: a 5 euro spare part that stops a machine has the priority of the machine


A task is as important as what waits for it.

title: Lecture IV: Scheduling
section: With dependencies, there is often no quick recipe
text:
With dependencies, there is often no quick recipe


For deadlines, waiting time and value, sorting is enough
Add dependencies, and for many goals nobody knows a fast way to find the best plan
In practice: good rules of thumb, or software that searches for a good plan


A good plan now beats a perfect plan too late.

Notes
In computer science terms these problems are NP-hard (NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time): no known algorithm finds the best plan in reasonable time once the task list grows, and this is true for most scheduling problems. Waiting time with dependencies is one example. The exception with deadlines: Lawler’s algorithm (1968) finds the best order for the worst delay with dependencies by filling the schedule from the back, always placing the task without successors that has the latest deadline last. It is no longer on the slides. Heuristics are rules that give good, but not provably optimal schedules.

A morning with seven tasks
It is 8:00. These tasks arrive during the morning:

Email A            8:00    20min      9:00

text:
In real time: switch only for an earlier deadline
Rule:

Always work on the task with the earliest deadline
A new task with an earlier deadline interrupts the current one
Otherwise, stick to the current task

This works for any goal: switch only if the new task beats the current one.

Notes
Equal deadline: if a new task has the same deadline as the current task, you can choose either. But because of the cost of context switching, you should stick with the current task.

Every time you switch tasks, you clear your desk for three books and set it up again
The switch itself produces nothing
Switch often enough, and switching is all you do

Back to the desk from Lecture III: the three books on the desk are what we have in mind for the current task. A switch means putting them back and fetching the books for the next task. The book calls this a context switch, and its cost is the time spent on the switch itself.

Explore gathers information, exploit uses it


Explore


Definition: Gathering new information
Risk: Unknown outcomes
Example: Trying that new sushi place



Exploit


Definition: Using known information
Risk: Missing better options
Example: Your go-to pizza joint










In any given moment you can only do one of the two.





The fundamental trade-off: explore and exploit are mutually exclusive choices in any given moment. You can’t have your cake and eat it too. Rule of thumb: win-stay, lose-shift1

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: A fair estimate: Laplace’s rule of succession
text:
A fair estimate: Laplace’s rule of succession

First we need a fair estimate of each machine
The plain win rate is extreme after few pulls: 1 win out of 1 pull looks like 100%, 0 out of 0 is undefined
Laplace (18th century) suggested a fairer estimate: after \(w\) wins and \(l\) losses, the chance of a win is about


\[\mathbb{E}[\text{win}] = \frac{w + 1}{w + l + 2}\]



In words: add one imagined win and one imagined loss, then take the share of wins


Pierre-Simon Laplace suggested this rule in the 18th century. The two added pulls keep the estimate away from 0 and 1 when we have seen very few pulls. The rule estimates how good a machine is; it does not tell us when to stop exploring.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Try it: machines A, B and C by Laplace
text:
Try it: machines A, B and C by Laplace
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{win}] = \frac{w + 1}{w + l + 2}\]
Question: What is E[B], E[A] and E[C]? Which machine looks better by this estimate?

E[B] = (1 + 1) / (2 + 2) = 0.50
E[A] = (9 + 1) / (15 + 2) = 10/17 ≈ 0.59
E[C] = (0 + 1) / (0 + 2) = 0.50, even though C was never played


Laplace gives unknown options a fair chance and avoids estimates of 0% or 100% after a few pulls.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Bellman: calculate backwards from the last pull
text:
Bellman: calculate backwards from the last pull

Richard Bellman found the exact solution for a known interval
Start at the final pull: with no future left, simply exploit
Then calculate backwards the best choice in every earlier situation


A few years after win-stay lose-shift, Richard Bellman found an exact solution for all cases with finite and known intervals. The question is when to stop exploring and start exploiting. The solution uses dynamic programming: start at the final pull and calculate backwards what the best choice is in every possible situation. This works because the last pull is easy.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Bellman needs to know how long you stay
text:
Bellman needs to know how long you stay

The calculation grows fast with many arms and a long interval
Worse: we usually don’t know how long we stay in the casino
So the bandit problem seemed to have no practical solution


The calculation of the optimal strategy is very extensive when there are many arms and a long interval. And the approach does not help in many scenarios, because we do not know the exact length of the interval. At this point it looked like the multi-armed bandit problem would remain a problem without a solution.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Gittins: a drug-trial problem at Unilever1
text:
Gittins: a drug-trial problem at Unilever1

In the 1970s, Unilever had several new compounds that might work as drugs
One test = one patient. Improvement = win, no improvement = loss
Testing costs time and money, and nobody knows in advance which compound is best
Unilever asked the mathematician John Gittins: which compound should we test next, and when should we stop testing?
Gittins saw that this is exactly our casino: each compound is a slot machine with an unknown win rate

For more details see Gittins, J. (1979) ‘Bandit Processes and Dynamic Allocation Indices’, Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series B (Methodological).

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Gittins discounts the future

His answer: give every machine a single number, computed only from its own wins and losses, and always play the machine with the highest number. That number is the Gittins index.
Earlier solutions needed a known interval
Gittins instead counts future wins less than immediate ones (discount factor), like future cash flows
Money: Money today can earn interest
Everyday life: Tonight’s dinner beats the same dinner next week
So any interval length works, even an endless one

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Back to machine A and B
text:
Back to machine A and B

The Gittins index works for every multi-armed bandit problem
Let’s consider our two machines one last time:

Machine A: 15 pulls, 9 wins, 6 losses
Machine B: 2 pulls, 1 win, 1 loss

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Gittins Index: the math behind the table
text:
Gittins Index: the math behind the table
\[G_i(s_i, f_i) := \sup_{\tau \geq 1} \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \beta^t \cdot r_i^t \middle| s_i, f_i\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \beta^t\right]}\]
In words: imagine a second machine that pays out at a fixed, known rate. The index is the rate that machine would need, so that you’d be indifferent between the two. The more uncertain a machine, the higher its index, because it might turn out great.







Too complex to calculate by hand, and you don’t need to: just use the lookup table!

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Higher index, better choice

Core idea: “What’s the best possible average reward from this option?”
Higher index = better choice
Less-tested options get an exploration bonus, that’s why machine B wins
The index balances exploration and exploitation automatically

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Where bandits run today

Online advertising: which of thousands of ads to show to this visitor, learning from every click
Streaming services: which thumbnail or recommendation to show, tested on millions of viewers
Website testing: two versions of a page, and the better one gets more visitors while the test is still running
Clinical trials: adaptive trials assign more patients to the treatment that works best so far


The same trade-off as in our casino, decided millions of times a day.

These systems use bandit algorithms in the spirit of Gittins, often simpler variants such as Thompson sampling or UCB. The point for us: explore and exploit is not a thought experiment, it runs the digital economy.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Which rule when?

Both outcomes known: choose the higher expected value
E(explore) unknown, interval known: Bellman (backward calculation)
E(explore) unknown, interval unknown: Gittins index


Three situations, three tools. If both outcomes are known, there is nothing to explore. If the interval is known, Bellman’s backward calculation gives the exact answer. If the interval is unknown, the Gittins index does.

section: Win-stay makes sense, lose-shift is too hasty
text:
Win-stay makes sense, lose-shift is too hasty


Win-stay

If you win, pull the same arm again
The arm has just become more attractive


Lose-shift

Switching after every loss is a rash move
Your favorite restaurant, tenth visit: always great, today disappointing
Should you never go back?

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Easy answers come with problems


Win-stay lose-shift penalizes losses too much
It ignores the interval
But it was a good start for better approaches

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: A fair estimate: Laplace’s rule of succession
text:
A fair estimate: Laplace’s rule of succession


First we need a fair estimate of each machine
The plain win rate is extreme after few pulls: 1 win out of 1 pull looks like 100%, 0 out of 0 is undefined
Laplace (18th century) suggested a fairer estimate: after \(w\) wins and \(l\) losses, the chance of a win is about


\[\mathbb{E}[\text{win}] = \frac{w + 1}{w + l + 2}\]

In words: add one imagined win and one imagined loss, then take the share of wins


Notes
Pierre-Simon Laplace suggested this rule in the 18th century. The two added pulls keep the estimate away from 0 and 1 when we have seen very few pulls. The rule estimates how good a machine is; it does not tell us when to stop exploring.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Try it: machines A, B and C by Laplace
text:
Try it: machines A, B and C by Laplace
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{win}] = \frac{w + 1}{w + l + 2}\]
Question: What is E[B], E[A] and E[C]? Which machine looks better by this estimate?


E[B] = (1 + 1) / (2 + 2) = 0.50
E[A] = (9 + 1) / (15 + 2) = 10/17 ≈ 0.59
E[C] = (0 + 1) / (0 + 2) = 0.50, even though C was never played



Laplace gives unknown options a fair chance and avoids estimates of 0% or 100% after a few pulls.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Laplace estimates for wins and losses

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Bellman: calculate backwards from the last pull
text:
Bellman: calculate backwards from the last pull


Richard Bellman found the exact solution for a known interval
Start at the final pull: with no future left, simply exploit
Then calculate backwards the best choice in every earlier situation



Notes
A few years after win-stay lose-shift, Richard Bellman found an exact solution for all cases with finite and known intervals. The question is when to stop exploring and start exploiting. The solution uses dynamic programming: start at the final pull and calculate backwards what the best choice is in every possible situation. This works because the last pull is easy.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Bellman needs to know how long you stay
text:
Bellman needs to know how long you stay


The calculation grows fast with many arms and a long interval
Worse: we usually don’t know how long we stay in the casino
So the bandit problem seemed to have no practical solution



Notes
The calculation of the optimal strategy is very extensive when there are many arms and a long interval. And the approach does not help in many scenarios, because we do not know the exact length of the interval. At this point it looked like the multi-armed bandit problem would remain a problem without a solution.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Gittins: a drug-trial problem at Unilever4
text:
Gittins: a drug-trial problem at Unilever4


In the 1970s, Unilever had several new compounds that might work as drugs
One test = one patient. Improvement = win, no improvement = loss
Testing costs time and money, and nobody knows in advance which compound is best
Unilever asked the mathematician John Gittins: which compound should we test next, and when should we stop testing?
Gittins saw that this is exactly our casino: each compound is a slot machine with an unknown win rate

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Gittins discounts the future


His answer: give every machine a single number, computed only from its own wins and losses, and always play the machine with the highest number. That number is the Gittins index.
Earlier solutions needed a known interval
Gittins instead counts future wins less than immediate ones (discount factor), like future cash flows
Money: Money today can earn interest
Everyday life: Tonight’s dinner beats the same dinner next week
So any interval length works, even an endless one

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Back to machine A and B
text:
Back to machine A and B


The Gittins index works for every multi-armed bandit problem
Let’s consider our two machines one last time:

Machine A: 15 pulls, 9 wins, 6 losses
Machine B: 2 pulls, 1 win, 1 loss

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: The Gittins index as a lookup table

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Machine A or B by the Gittins index?
text:
Machine A or B by the Gittins index?


Machine B (0.6346) beats machine A (0.6300)
Clear win-stay pattern, relaxed lose-shift pattern
At (0,0) we see the exploration bonus

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
section: Gittins Index: the math behind the table
text:
Gittins Index: the math behind the table
\[G_i(s_i, f_i) := \sup_{\tau \geq 1} \frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \beta^t \cdot r_i^t \middle| s_i, f_i\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\tau-1} \beta^t\right]}\]
In words: imagine a second machine that pays out at a fixed, known rate. The index is the rate that machine would need, so that you’d be indifferent between the two. The more uncertain a machine, the higher its index, because it might turn out great.







Too complex to calculate by hand, and you don’t need to: just use the lookup table!

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Higher index, better choice


Core idea: “What’s the best possible average reward from this option?”
Higher index = better choice
Less-tested options get an exploration bonus, that’s why machine B wins
The index balances exploration and exploitation automatically

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Where bandits run today


Online advertising: which of thousands of ads to show to this visitor, learning from every click
Streaming services: which thumbnail or recommendation to show, tested on millions of viewers
Website testing: two versions of a page, and the better one gets more visitors while the test is still running
Clinical trials: adaptive trials assign more patients to the treatment that works best so far


The same trade-off as in our casino, decided millions of times a day.

Notes
These systems use bandit algorithms in the spirit of Gittins, often simpler variants such as Thompson sampling or UCB. The point for us: explore and exploit is not a thought experiment, it runs the digital economy.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Which rule when?


Both outcomes known: choose the higher expected value
E(explore) unknown, interval known: Bellman (backward calculation)
E(explore) unknown, interval unknown: Gittins index



Notes
Three situations, three tools. If both outcomes are known, there is nothing to explore. If the interval is known, Bellman’s backward calculation gives the exact answer. If the interval is unknown, the Gittins index does.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
What we covered


The dilemma: try something new or stick with what works
Every choice between the new and the known trades information against reward.


Time decides: why the end of the interval changes everything
The more time is left, the more exploring pays off; near the end, exploit what you know.


Smart strategies: from rules of thumb to the Gittins index
Simple rules like win-stay, lose-shift help, but better strategies weigh both what you know and how uncertain you still are.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Why it matters

You have 45 minutes for lunch: the new restaurant or your reliable favorite? Companies face the same choice every day: a new supplier or the proven one, a new marketing channel or the one that works, a new film or another sequel.

title: Lecture II: Explore & Exploit
text:
Explore early.
Exploit late.

title: Programming: Everyday Decision-Making Algorithms
text:
Course Description
This course explores the intersection of computer science and everyday life by examining how algorithms can be applied to improve decision-making in various contexts. Inspired by the book “Algorithms to Live By” by Brian Christian and Tom Griffiths, the course will cover optimal stopping, explore and exploit, caching, scheduling, randomness and computational kindness, with an outlook on topics such as game theory, providing both theoretical foundations and practical programming exercises. The course consists of lectures and exercises.

title: Programming: Everyday Decision-Making Algorithms
text:
Learning Outcomes
Our broad goal is to equip students with the ability to get to grips with algorithmic thinking. We want to enable students to independently apply methods and concepts from algorithms to solve their everyday practical problems while also providing a brief introduction into programming with Python.
Upon completion of the course, students will:

understand fundamental algorithms and their applications to everyday problems
develop the ability to model real-world scenarios using algorithmic thinking
implement simple algorithms in Python to solve practical problems
analyze the efficiency and effectiveness of different algorithms in various contexts

Please note that this course is specifically designed for business students. That is, it is not required to have any advanced knowledge or experience in programming to attend this course. The teaching format will make it possible to account for different levels of programming skills such that every student can take the most out of the course.

title: Programming: Everyday Decision-Making Algorithms
text:
Course Structure
The course is based on a hands-on approach with a two-fold structure:

Lectures: In the lectures, we will introduce and discuss concepts and illustrate them in reproducible examples.
Hands-on Tutorials: Students will apply the concepts from the lecture in Jupyter notebooks, while simultaneously learning the basics of Python.

The course is not graded and can only be passed/failed. To pass, you need:

Attendance: at least 75% of the lectures.
Assignments: two assignments, each on an algorithmic problem from the course. At least 50% of the solutions must be correct.
Presentation: a short final presentation of an implemented prototype in the last lecture, followed by a discussion in class.

All assignments are due by the end of the quarter, but earlier submissions are highly encouraged. You can work in groups of up to three students.
You can find more information on the course contents in the syllabus.

text:
The big picture: five things you will use








What
In simple words

Python
A programming language
We write our programs in Python

An app to write code, like Word for text
This is where you write and run your code

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 1: Install VS Code
Where: your web browser
Why: VS Code is the app you will work in for the whole course. Apps like this are called IDEs (Integrated Development Environments): one place to write code, run it and find mistakes.
Do: Go to code.visualstudio.com and download VS Code for your system.

macOSWindows



Open the downloaded file. A file called Visual Studio Code appears.
Drag it into your Applications folder.
Open it from Applications. If your Mac asks whether you want to open an app from the internet, click Open.




Open the downloaded installer.
Accept the agreement and keep the default settings. Make sure “Add to PATH” is ticked.
Click Install, then Finish.




Check: VS Code opens and shows a welcome page.

title: Installation Guide
section: Step 2: Add the Python and Jupyter extensions
text:
Step 2: Add the Python and Jupyter extensions
Where: VS Code
Why: Out of the box, VS Code doesn’t know Python or notebooks. Extensions are small add-ons that teach it.
Do:

Click the Extensions icon on the left side (four small squares).
Search for Python and click Install on the one by Microsoft.
Search for Jupyter and click Install on the one by Microsoft.

Check: Both extensions show “Installed” or a gear icon instead of an Install button.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 3: Create your course folder
Where: Finder (macOS) or File Explorer (Windows)
Why: Everything for this course lives in one folder. That keeps things tidy, and Python works best when each project has its own folder.

macOSWindows


Open Finder, go to your home folder (the one with the house icon) and create a new folder called programming-course.


Open File Explorer, click into the address bar at the top, type %USERPROFILE% and press Enter. This opens your user folder. Create a new folder there called programming-course.
Please don’t put it in a OneDrive folder. Syncing can break the setup.



Do in VS Code: Click File → Open Folder…, select programming-course and click Open. If VS Code asks whether you trust the authors of the files, click Yes, I trust the authors.
Check: On the left side of VS Code, you see the name PROGRAMMING-COURSE at the top.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 4: Open the terminal
Where: VS Code
Why: The terminal is where you type commands. You type a command, press Enter, and the computer answers with text. We only need a few commands, and you can copy them from this page.
Do: In the menu bar, click Terminal → New Terminal. A panel opens at the bottom of VS Code.

macOSWindows


The terminal shows a line ending with %. That’s where you type.


The terminal shows a line starting with PS and ending with >. PS means PowerShell, which is exactly what we need. If you don’t see PS, click the small arrow next to the + in the terminal panel and choose PowerShell.



Good to know:

Copy a command from this page, paste it into the terminal and press Enter.
Paste with Cmd + V (macOS) or Ctrl + V or a right-click (Windows).
Some commands take a few seconds. Wait until the line with % or > is back before typing the next one.

Check: You see a terminal at the bottom of VS Code, and its line mentions programming-course.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 5: Install uv
Where: the terminal in VS Code
Why: uv is a helper that installs Python for you and keeps each project clean. You only install it once.
Do: Copy the command for your system and press Enter.

macOSWindows


curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh


powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"









WarningRestart required



The terminal only learns about new tools when VS Code starts fresh.

macOSWindows


Quit VS Code with Cmd + Q. Closing the window is not enough.


Close all VS Code windows.





Open VS Code again. Check: The top left must show PROGRAMMING-COURSE again. If it doesn’t, click File → Open Recent → programming-course. Then open a new terminal with Terminal → New Terminal.
Check: Type this and press Enter:
uv --version
You should see something like uv 0.12.0. The exact number doesn’t matter.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 6: Install Python
Where: the terminal in VS Code
Why: This installs the Python language itself. Everyone in the course uses the same version, so the code works the same for all.
Do:
uv python install 3.13
Check: The terminal says that Python 3.13 was installed, or that it is already installed. Both are fine.

title: Installation Guide
section: Step 7: Turn your folder into a Python project
text:
Step 7: Turn your folder into a Python project
Where: the terminal in VS Code, inside programming-course
Why: This tells uv: “this folder is a Python project”. uv creates a few files it needs to keep track of things.
Check first: The terminal must be inside your course folder. Type this and press Enter:

macOSWindows


pwd


Get-Location



The answer must end with programming-course. If it doesn’t: close the terminal (the bin icon in the terminal panel), open the folder with File → Open Recent → programming-course, and open a new terminal with Terminal → New Terminal.
Do: Run this command:
uv init --no-package --python 3.13
This creates a simple project with a main.py and Python 3.13 as its minimum version. (--no-package matters: since uv 0.12, plain uv init creates a src/ folder without main.py instead.)
New files appear on the left in VS Code. You don’t need to touch them:

main.py: a tiny example program
pyproject.toml: the list of what your project needs
.python-version: which Python version the project uses

Check: Run the example program:
uv run python main.py
You should see Hello from programming-course!. Congratulations, you just ran your first Python program!

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 8: Add notebook support
Where: the terminal in VS Code
Why: Notebooks need two extra helpers. The first one lets notebooks use the Python of your project, the second one adds the notebook tools.
Do:
uv add --dev ipykernel
uv add jupyter
Check: The terminal lists a lot of installed packages and ends without an error. You see a folder .venv on the left. That’s your project’s own Python environment.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 9: Your first notebook
Where: VS Code
Why: This checks that everything works together, before you start with the tutorials.
Do:

Press Cmd + Shift + P (macOS) or Ctrl + Shift + P (Windows). A search bar opens at the top.
Type Create: New Jupyter Notebook and press Enter.
Click Select Kernel in the top right corner. The kernel is the Python that runs your notebook.
Choose Python Environments, then the one that says .venv and Python 3.13. If you don’t see Python Environments, click Select Another Kernel… first.
Click into the first cell, type print("Hello") and press Shift + Enter.

Check: Below the cell, you see Hello. Everything works!
If VS Code asks to install extensions at any point, click Install.

title: Installation Guide
text:
Step 10: Open a tutorial
Where: your web browser, then VS Code
Do:

Open a tutorial on the course website.
On the right side under Other Formats, click Jupyter to download the notebook.
Move the downloaded file into your programming-course folder.
Open it in VS Code by clicking it on the left.
If VS Code asks for a kernel, choose the same .venv with Python 3.13 as in Step 9.

You’re ready for the tutorials!

title: Installation Guide
text:
Something doesn’t work?







Problem
What to do




uv is “not found” or “not recognized”
Restart VS Code as in Step 5 (macOS: Cmd + Q, Windows: close all windows). On Windows, check that the terminal says PS.


main.py can’t be found
Your terminal is probably in the wrong folder. Check the folder and the terminal as in Step 7, then run uv init --no-package --python 3.13 again in the right folder. If uv then says the project is already initialized, see the next row. If uv init ran in a different folder by mistake: don’t delete anything, ask us.


uv says the project is already initialized
Your project already exists, don’t run uv init again. If you see main.py, continue with uv run python main.py. If there is a src/ folder, see the row below. If neither exists, create a new file main.py on the left (New File icon) with the line print("Hello from programming-course!"), save it and run uv run python main.py.


There is a folder src/ but no main.py
You ran uv init without --no-package. That’s fine: test with uv run programming-course instead. It should print Hello from programming-course!. Then continue with Step 8.


uv says the Python version is incompatible with the project
Open pyproject.toml in VS Code and change the line requires-python to requires-python = ">=3.13". Save the file, then run uv python pin 3.13 and uv sync.


Windows says scripts are disabled
Run Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Scope Process, then repeat Step 5.


.venv doesn’t appear under Select Kernel
Press Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + P, type Developer: Reload Window, press Enter, try again.


The notebook shows a different Python than 3.13
Click on the kernel name in the top right and choose the .venv one.


uv self update fails on a Mac
If you installed uv with Homebrew, use brew upgrade uv instead.


Anything else
Ask us! Guessing usually takes longer than asking.

Why this matters: optimal stopping is everywhere in life, from hiring decisions to finding apartments to choosing when to sell stocks. Today we learn the mathematical strategy that maximizes the chance of making the best choice.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: The Secretary Problem: hire now or keep looking?
text:
The Secretary Problem: hire now or keep looking?


You are hiring a secretary and interview candidates one by one
After each interview: hire or continue searching
Once you reject a candidate, you cannot go back
How to maximize the chance of hiring the best candidate?



Notes
The name comes from the 1960s. The problem is about finding the best candidate, not about secretaries. It is also known as the marriage problem or the dowry problem.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The setup in three lines

We have n candidates and interview them one by one
After each one: hire or continue searching
We can only rank candidates relative to those we have already seen (ordinal ranking)

Question: Where in your life can you say “this one is better than that one”, but not “this one is worth 7 out of 10”?

Notes
Ordinal ranking: we can say which of two candidates is better, but we do not have a score or an absolute scale. This is what makes the problem hard, we never know how good the best candidate could be.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
Two ways to fail
Question: Any idea how we could fail?

Reject everyone and never hire: stopping too late
Hire someone too early: stopping too early

decide when to stop?

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: Look at the first 37%, then leap
text:
Look at the first 37%, then leap


Look at the first 37% of candidates without hiring anyone
Remember the best candidate so far
Leap: hire the next candidate who is better than that one
This finds the very best candidate in 37% of all cases



Notes
This is the mathematically optimal strategy. It means we still fail 63% of the time, but this is the best we can possibly do. The 37% holds for a large number of candidates; with only a few candidates, the chance is even higher.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: Picking at random gets worse with every candidate
text:
Picking at random gets worse with every candidate
Chance of the best candidate if we pick one at random:

1 candidate: 100%, 2 candidates: 50%, 3 candidates: 33%
4 candidates: 25%, 5 candidates: 20%

Question: Do you see the pattern?
Pattern: 1/n. Look-and-leap never drops below 37%, however many candidates there are.

Notes
Random choice gets worse with every extra candidate, because each individual candidate is less likely to be the best. The look-and-leap strategy does not have this problem: its success chance never drops below 37%, however many candidates there are, and with few candidates it is even higher.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
Why 37%?

Look at the first share \(x\) of candidates, then leap
Chance of getting the best: about \(-x \ln x\)1
In words: look longer and your benchmark improves, but the best may already be gone
Largest at \(x = 1/e \approx 37\%\)2

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: Let the computer try it out
text:
Let the computer try it out


Shuffle 100 candidates into a random order
Look at the first 37 and remember the best one
Hire the first candidate who beats that benchmark
Check: did we get the very best?
Repeat 10,000 times and count how often we won

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The same idea in code

import random
random.seed(42)

def one_round(n=100, look=37):
    candidates = list(range(n))          # n - 1 is the best
    random.shuffle(candidates)
    benchmark = max(candidates[:look])   # best of the look phase
    for c in candidates[look:]:
        if c > benchmark:                # first one who beats it
            return c == n - 1            # did we hire the best?
    return False                         # nobody beat the benchmark

wins = sum(one_round() for _ in range(10_000))
print(f"Best candidate found in {wins / 10_000:.1%} of rounds")

Best candidate found in 37.5% of rounds








No worries if you don’t understand every line yet. By the end of the course, you will.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
Real life changes the assumptions
So far, we made some strong simplifications. Real life is messier.
Question: What could be different in real life?


The other person can say no
You can go back to someone you passed
You know how good an option is, not just how it compares
You have a fixed time, not a fixed number of options
One failure can mean losing everything
Looking costs time and effort

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you can be rejected?
text:
What if you can be rejected?
Question: In dating, the other person can also say no. Earlier or later than 37%?


50% chance of rejection: leap at 25%
Formula: \(q^{\frac{1}{1-q}}\), \(q\) = chance that your offer is accepted3
In words: the more often you hear “no”, the earlier you leap



Notes
Life lesson: higher risk of rejection means we should be less picky. With q = 0.5 the formula gives 0.5 to the power of 2, that is 25%. If offers are always accepted (q close to 1), the formula gives back the familiar 1/e.
Example from Brian Christian: searching from age 18 to 40, the 37% rule says get serious at 26.1. With many rejections, start at 23.5.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you can go back?
text:
What if you can go back?
Question: You can return to someone you passed on, but they might say no. Look longer or shorter?


Going back works only half the time: look at 61%4, then leap
If nobody better comes, return to the best you passed
In words: a second chance makes it safe to look longer



Notes
Example from the book: an immediate offer is always accepted, a belated one only with 50%. The safety net of going back shifts the look phase from 37% to 61%.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you know how good an option is?
text:
What if you know how good an option is?
Question: Test scores, prices per square meter: do we still need a look phase?


Example: you know test scores, or the price per square meter of a flat
No look phase needed: take the first option above a threshold
The threshold drops as fewer options remain
Chance of getting the very best rises to 58%5



Notes
This is the “full information” version. With absolute scores and a known distribution, you don’t need to learn a benchmark first. The threshold starts high and falls as you run out of options.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
What if time is fixed?
Example: one year to find a flat, viewings come as they come
Question: How should we adapt our strategy?


Same principle: look for the first 37% of the time6, then leap
The number of options is not fixed: the harder we search, the more options we see



Notes
This holds if options arrive evenly over time. We can also decide how intensively we search, for example by viewing more flats per week. Searching harder in the look phase improves the benchmark.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The burglar: when to retire?
Example: each break-in succeeds with chance \(q\), one failure means losing everything
Question: Does the answer depend on \(q\), and how?


Stop after about \(\frac{q}{1-q}\) successes
With \(q = 90\%\): retire after 9 break-ins7
Same logic for any streak that can end badly: a winning run in the casino, a project that keeps growing in risk

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
What do people actually do?


In about a dozen experiments, people leap earlier than the 37% rule suggests8
Question: Why might that be?
Searching costs time and effort, and the rule ignores that
If looking is expensive, leaping earlier can be the right choice



Notes
Experiments by Seale and Rapoport (1997). The 37% rule assumes that looking is free. In real life, every viewing or interview costs time, so stopping a bit earlier is often rational, not a mistake.
Side note for drivers: an increase in occupancy from 90 to 95% doubles the search time for all drivers. Each variation changes the rule a little, but the structure stays: options come one at a time, and you cannot go back.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
What we covered


The problem: choosing the best when options come one at a time
Many decisions share one structure: options arrive one at a time, and there is no going back.


The rule: look first, then leap
Looking at the first 37% and then taking the first better option gives the best possible chance of picking the very best: 37%.


Real life: when the assumptions change
The rule adapts to real life: leap earlier if you can be rejected or looking is costly, wait longer if you can go back.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
Footnotes


Where does this come from? You win if the best candidate comes after your look phase and nobody before them beats your benchmark. That happens exactly when the best of all earlier candidates was in your look phase. Adding up these chances for every position, with many candidates, gives about \(-x \ln x\), where \(x\) is the share of candidates you only look at.↩︎
To find the best look phase, we only need to know where \(-x \ln x\) reaches its maximum. Setting its derivative \(-\ln x - 1\) to zero gives \(x = 1/e \approx 37\%\), where \(e \approx 2.718\) is the base of the natural logarithm. For the full story, see Ferguson, T.S. (1989) ‘Who solved the secretary problem?’, Statistical Science, 4(3).↩︎
How it works: after the look phase, you ask everyone who beats all earlier candidates, and each says yes with chance \(q\). You get the best only if the best says yes and everyone you asked before said no. More rejections mean you use up more candidates after the look phase, so you have to start earlier. The stated formula is the best look phase, for example 25% when \(q = 50\%\). As in the basic problem, your chance of getting the best equals the look phase. With \(q\) close to 1, it gives back 37%.↩︎
Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.↩︎
Gilbert, J.P. & Mosteller, F. (1966). Recognizing the maximum of a sequence. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 61(313), 35–73.↩︎
Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.↩︎
Ferguson, T.S. Optimal Stopping and Applications. Lecture notes, University of California, Los Angeles, https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tom/Stopping/. The rule assumes the same haul every time: stop once your total haul is worth more than what you would expect to gain from one more attempt.↩︎

text:
The Secretary Problem: hire now or keep looking?

You are hiring a secretary and interview candidates one by one
After each interview: hire or continue searching
Once you reject a candidate, you cannot go back
How to maximize the chance of hiring the best candidate?


The name comes from the 1960s. The problem is about finding the best candidate, not about secretaries. It is also known as the marriage problem or the dowry problem.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The setup in three lines

We have n candidates and interview them one by one
After each one: hire or continue searching
We can only rank candidates relative to those we have already seen (ordinal ranking)


Question: Where in your life can you say “this one is better than that one”, but not “this one is worth 7 out of 10”?

Ordinal ranking: we can say which of two candidates is better, but we do not have a score or an absolute scale. This is what makes the problem hard, we never know how good the best candidate could be.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
Two ways to fail
Question: Any idea how we could fail?


Reject everyone and never hire: stopping too late
Hire someone too early: stopping too early

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: Look at the first 37%, then leap
text:
Look at the first 37%, then leap

Look at the first 37% of candidates without hiring anyone
Remember the best candidate so far
Leap: hire the next candidate who is better than that one
This finds the very best candidate in 37% of all cases


This is the mathematically optimal strategy. It means we still fail 63% of the time, but this is the best we can possibly do. The 37% holds for a large number of candidates; with only a few candidates, the chance is even higher.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: Picking at random gets worse with every candidate
text:
Picking at random gets worse with every candidate
Chance of the best candidate if we pick one at random:

1 candidate: 100%, 2 candidates: 50%, 3 candidates: 33%
4 candidates: 25%, 5 candidates: 20%


Question: Do you see the pattern?


Pattern: 1/n. Look-and-leap never drops below 37%, however many candidates there are.

Random choice gets worse with every extra candidate, because each individual candidate is less likely to be the best. The look-and-leap strategy does not have this problem: its success chance never drops below 37%, however many candidates there are, and with few candidates it is even higher.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
Why 37%?

Look at the first share \(x\) of candidates, then leap
Chance of getting the best: about \(-x \ln x\)1
In words: look longer and your benchmark improves, but the best may already be gone
Largest at \(x = 1/e \approx 37\%\)2

Where does this come from? You win if the best candidate comes after your look phase and nobody before them beats your benchmark. That happens exactly when the best of all earlier candidates was in your look phase. Adding up these chances for every position, with many candidates, gives about \(-x \ln x\), where \(x\) is the share of candidates you only look at.To find the best look phase, we only need to know where \(-x \ln x\) reaches its maximum. Setting its derivative \(-\ln x - 1\) to zero gives \(x = 1/e \approx 37\%\), where \(e \approx 2.718\) is the base of the natural logarithm. For the full story, see Ferguson, T.S. (1989) ‘Who solved the secretary problem?’, Statistical Science, 4(3).

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: Let the computer try it out
text:
Let the computer try it out

Shuffle 100 candidates into a random order
Look at the first 37 and remember the best one
Hire the first candidate who beats that benchmark
Check: did we get the very best?
Repeat 10,000 times and count how often we won

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The same idea in code

import random
random.seed(42)

def one_round(n=100, look=37):
    candidates = list(range(n))          # n - 1 is the best
    random.shuffle(candidates)
    benchmark = max(candidates[:look])   # best of the look phase
    for c in candidates[look:]:
        if c > benchmark:                # first one who beats it
            return c == n - 1            # did we hire the best?
    return False                         # nobody beat the benchmark

wins = sum(one_round() for _ in range(10_000))
print(f"Best candidate found in {wins / 10_000:.1%} of rounds")



Best candidate found in 37.5% of rounds








No worries if you don’t understand every line yet. By the end of the course, you will.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
Real life changes the assumptions
So far, we made some strong simplifications. Real life is messier.

Question: What could be different in real life?



The other person can say no
You can go back to someone you passed
You know how good an option is, not just how it compares
You have a fixed time, not a fixed number of options
One failure can mean losing everything
Looking costs time and effort

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you can be rejected?
text:
What if you can be rejected?
Question: In dating, the other person can also say no. Earlier or later than 37%?

50% chance of rejection: leap at 25%
Formula: \(q^{\frac{1}{1-q}}\), \(q\) = chance that your offer is accepted1
In words: the more often you hear “no”, the earlier you leap


Life lesson: higher risk of rejection means we should be less picky. With q = 0.5 the formula gives 0.5 to the power of 2, that is 25%. If offers are always accepted (q close to 1), the formula gives back the familiar 1/e.
Example from Brian Christian: searching from age 18 to 40, the 37% rule says get serious at 26.1. With many rejections, start at 23.5.

How it works: after the look phase, you ask everyone who beats all earlier candidates, and each says yes with chance \(q\). You get the best only if the best says yes and everyone you asked before said no. More rejections mean you use up more candidates after the look phase, so you have to start earlier. The stated formula is the best look phase, for example 25% when \(q = 50\%\). As in the basic problem, your chance of getting the best equals the look phase. With \(q\) close to 1, it gives back 37%.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you can go back?
text:
What if you can go back?
Question: You can return to someone you passed on, but they might say no. Look longer or shorter?

Going back works only half the time: look at 61%1, then leap
If nobody better comes, return to the best you passed
In words: a second chance makes it safe to look longer


Example from the book: an immediate offer is always accepted, a belated one only with 50%. The safety net of going back shifts the look phase from 37% to 61%.

Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
section: What if you know how good an option is?
text:
What if you know how good an option is?
Question: Test scores, prices per square meter: do we still need a look phase?

Example: you know test scores, or the price per square meter of a flat
No look phase needed: take the first option above a threshold
The threshold drops as fewer options remain
Chance of getting the very best rises to 58%1


This is the “full information” version. With absolute scores and a known distribution, you don’t need to learn a benchmark first. The threshold starts high and falls as you run out of options.

Gilbert, J.P. & Mosteller, F. (1966). Recognizing the maximum of a sequence. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 61(313), 35–73.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
What if time is fixed?
Example: one year to find a flat, viewings come as they come

Question: How should we adapt our strategy?



Same principle: look for the first 37% of the time1, then leap
The number of options is not fixed: the harder we search, the more options we see


This holds if options arrive evenly over time. We can also decide how intensively we search, for example by viewing more flats per week. Searching harder in the look phase improves the benchmark.


Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
The burglar: when to retire?
Example: each break-in succeeds with chance \(q\), one failure means losing everything

Question: Does the answer depend on \(q\), and how?



Stop after about \(\frac{q}{1-q}\) successes
With \(q = 90\%\): retire after 9 break-ins1
Same logic for any streak that can end badly: a winning run in the casino, a project that keeps growing in risk


Ferguson, T.S. Optimal Stopping and Applications. Lecture notes, University of California, Los Angeles, https://www.math.ucla.edu/~tom/Stopping/. The rule assumes the same haul every time: stop once your total haul is worth more than what you would expect to gain from one more attempt.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
What do people actually do?

In about a dozen experiments, people leap earlier than the 37% rule suggests1
Question: Why might that be?
Searching costs time and effort, and the rule ignores that
If looking is expensive, leaping earlier can be the right choice


Experiments by Seale and Rapoport (1997). The 37% rule assumes that looking is free. In real life, every viewing or interview costs time, so stopping a bit earlier is often rational, not a mistake.
Side note for drivers: an increase in occupancy from 90 to 95% doubles the search time for all drivers. Each variation changes the rule a little, but the structure stays: options come one at a time, and you cannot go back.

Christian, B. & Griffiths, T. (2016). Algorithms to Live By. Henry Holt, Chapter 1.

title: Lecture I: Optimal Stopping
text:
What we covered


The problem: choosing the best when options come one at a time
Many decisions share one structure: options arrive one at a time, and there is no going back.


The rule: look first, then leap
Looking at the first 37% and then taking the first better option gives the best possible chance of picking the very best: 37%.


Real life: when the assumptions change
The rule adapts to real life: leap earlier if you can be rejected or looking is costly, wait longer if you can go back.

You visit flats in Hamburg. Each viewing, you must decide on the spot, and if you say no, the flat is gone. Choose too early and you miss better ones; wait too long and the best is behind you. Companies face the same problem when hiring, choosing suppliers or accepting offers.

It costs money

Notes
The trade-off behind the second point: size versus speed. The larger a storage, the longer it takes to find a thing in it. That holds for a cupboard, a warehouse and, as we will see, for computer memory.

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: A fast processor waiting for slow memory
text:
A fast processor waiting for slow memory


Processors got faster much more quickly than memory
Modern CPUs: billions of operations per second
But the data doesn’t arrive fast enough
Question: How would you solve this?




Make all memory fast? Far too expensive.
Better: keep the data you need most right next to the processor.



That small, fast memory is called a cache.1


Notes
The evolution of computer memory: computer science faced the same storage problem as our cupboard. In 1946 von Neumann’s team already expected a hierarchy of memories. Processors then became faster much more quickly than memory (Moore’s Law, 1965), so in 1965 Maurice Wilkes proposed a small, fast memory close to the processor (he called it a “slave memory”), the first cache. In 1995 Wulf and McKee called the growing gap the “Memory Wall”. The waiting itself is often called the von Neumann bottleneck, a term coined by John Backus in 1977.
