Fast memory is small, big memory is slow









A register is roughly ten million times faster than a hard disk. Question: Why not make everything that fast?

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Why not make everything fast?


Physics: larger memory sits further away, signals take longer, fast memory gets hot
Money: per gigabyte, cache memory costs many times more than a hard disk
Solution: several levels, each optimized for its job



Notes
Physical limits: larger memory sits further from the CPU, signals take longer to travel, and dense fast memory produces heat that must be dissipated. Economic limits: per gigabyte, fast cache memory costs many orders of magnitude more than a hard disk. The solution is a hierarchy with multiple cache levels, each optimized for different needs.

text:
LRU in practice


Least Recently Used (LRU) is the dominant strategy
Question: Why is this the better strategy?
Because the recent past predicts the near future
Temporal locality: what you used recently, you will likely need again soon
Books on your desk, apps opened today, people texted this morning
In Belady’s classic comparison, LRU came closest to the crystal ball2

So the most recently used files are always in front
A pile does the same: what you used last lies on top

Regional warehouses keep goods close to the customer

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Flooding and poisoning


Flooding: so many notifications that what matters gets pushed out. That is distraction.
Poisoning: false information lands on your desk and you rely on it without checking. That is misinformation.
Both work because attention is small and we trust what is right in front of us.



Notes
The terms come from computer security. Cache flooding is a form of Denial-of-Service attack: the system is overloaded with requests, important data is evicted, the system slows down or crashes. Cache poisoning plants false data in a cache, so later requests are answered with wrong content; DNS cache poisoning, for example, sends users to a fake website. Both exploit that a cache is small and is trusted without checking the original source.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Getting it back is expensive


After an interruption, it often takes 20+ minutes to get back on track5
Like a trip to the slowest memory: millions of times more expensive than staying at the desk
Technology and social media are designed to capture attention



Reflection: How many times did you check your phone during this lecture?


Notes
Five productivity killers, in cache terms. Overload: too much information at once, the cache capacity is exceeded. Exhaustion: too long without clearing out. Context switching: every interruption of flow costs often 20 minutes or more to get back on track. Distraction: cache flooding by constant notifications and social media. Misinformation: cache poisoning by fake news and misleading information. The result is less creativity, less critical thinking and less productivity.

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: What gets evicted: first the task, then your goals, then your values
text:
What gets evicted: first the task, then your goals, then your values


Spotlight: what you are doing right now
Starlight: your goals for this year
Daylight: your values, who you want to be6



LRU evicts what you haven’t touched for a long time. If your attention always goes to notifications, you first lose the task, then your goals, and in the end, Williams argues, yourself.


Notes
The three levels come from James Williams, a former Google strategist, quoted in Johann Hari’s “Stolen Focus”. Spotlight: immediate goals, your focus, what are you working on right now? Starlight: medium-term goals, your wishes, what matters this year? Daylight: long-term goals, your values, what defines your life direction?

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
What to do about it


Fewer interruptions: notifications off while you work, one thing at a time
Choose what gets in: be selective with news and feeds
Touch what matters: revisit your goals regularly, so they don’t get evicted



Want to dive deeper? Rolf Dobelli, The Not To-Do List, chapters 15, 46, 51 and 52. Johann Hari, Stolen Focus. And because news is a big source of distraction: Rolf Dobelli, Stop Reading the News.


Notes
More tips, in cache terms. Prioritize sleep, nutrition and mindful habits: they maintain cache performance. Take breaks: regular clearing out prevents exhaustion. Time-box your work: structure prevents overflow. Create protected time for deep work and a dedicated workspace: that prevents cache flooding. Meditation and exercise are maintenance routines for the cache. Treat your desk as a cache hierarchy: hot cache on the desk with only today’s tasks, warm cache in a nearby shelf or drawer with this week’s projects, cold storage in the archive or closet for everything else. If you haven’t used it recently, move it away. Distraction can hardly be avoided in today’s world, especially for managers, but it can be reduced, and awareness is the first step.

Notes
Key takeaways, the concepts: caching is universal, it applies to computers, organizations and human cognition. The fundamental trade-off: fast storage is small, large storage is slow. Protect your attention, it is your scarcest and most valuable resource. Apply caching principles to life: keep what you use, remove what you don’t.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Today in one sentence

When space is limited, keep close what you are likely to need next, and the best guide to that is what you used most recently.


Why it matters
Your cupboard is full, your desk is cluttered, your inbox overflows. Companies have the same problem: which goods sit next to the loading dock, which files stay on the fast server, which tasks get your attention today.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:

The problem: limited space, too much stuff
The solution: keep what you need close, clear out the rest

title: Lecture III: Caching

A quick question first

Question: How many of you have a messy desktop right now? Raise your hand!


Today’s lecture will explain why that matters more than you think…

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
A messy cupboard


Question: What would you do?

Sort it: similar things together
Keep what you use often within easy reach
Now you find things faster

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Organized, but full


Question: And now?

Get more space
Clear out







Better organization helps, but every storage has a finite capacity. More space helps, but it has limits too. Sooner or later we are left with the second option: clearing out. The rest of the lecture is about how to do that well.

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: Why not just buy more space?
text:
Why not just buy more space?



It costs money
Bigger storage is slower to search
Sooner or later it fills up again







The trade-off behind the second point: size versus speed. The larger a storage, the longer it takes to find a thing in it. That holds for a cupboard, a warehouse and, as we will see, for computer memory.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Who else has this problem?

Warehouses
Computers
Email inboxes
Smartphones
Our brain?!

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: A fast processor waiting for slow memory
text:
A fast processor waiting for slow memory

Processors got faster much more quickly than memory
Modern CPUs: billions of operations per second
But the data doesn’t arrive fast enough
Question: How would you solve this?


Make all memory fast? Far too expensive.
Better: keep the data you need most right next to the processor.


That small, fast memory is called a cache.1


The evolution of computer memory: computer science faced the same storage problem as our cupboard. In 1946 von Neumann’s team already expected a hierarchy of memories. Processors then became faster much more quickly than memory (Moore’s Law, 1965), so in 1965 Maurice Wilkes proposed a small, fast memory close to the processor (he called it a “slave memory”), the first cache. In 1995 Wulf and McKee called the growing gap the “Memory Wall”. The waiting itself is often called the von Neumann bottleneck, a term coined by John Backus in 1977.

Burks, A. W., Goldstine, H. H., & von Neumann, J. (1946). Preliminary discussion of the logical design of an electronic computing instrument. Wilkes, M. V. (1965). Slave memories and dynamic storage allocation. Wulf, W. A., & McKee, S. A. (1995). Hitting the memory wall. See also Christian & Griffiths (2016), ch. 4.

The cache: a hierarchy of memories

A hierarchical memory system


L1 Cache: Tiny but ultra-fast (kilobytes)
L2/L3 Cache: Larger, still fast (megabytes)
RAM: Main workspace (gigabytes)
Storage: Huge but slow (terabytes)


Like a library…

text:
Like a library: closer is faster and smaller




Library storage (millions of books, mass storage)
Subject shelves (thousands of books, RAM)
Your desk (a few borrowed books, L2)
Short-term memory (current page, L1)


Closer = Faster = Smaller

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: Fast memory is small, big memory is slow
text:
Fast memory is small, big memory is slow









A register is roughly ten million times faster than a hard disk. Question: Why not make everything that fast?

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Why not make everything fast?

Physics: larger memory sits further away, signals take longer, fast memory gets hot
Money: per gigabyte, cache memory costs many times more than a hard disk
Solution: several levels, each optimized for its job


Physical limits: larger memory sits further from the CPU, signals take longer to travel, and dense fast memory produces heat that must be dissipated. Economic limits: per gigabyte, fast cache memory costs many orders of magnitude more than a hard disk. The solution is a hierarchy with multiple cache levels, each optimized for different needs.

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: So we have to clear out. But what goes?
text:
So we have to clear out. But what goes?

True for cupboards, computers, brains…
But what stays and what goes?

A desk for three books



You study at a desk with room for three books
All other books are on a shelf across the room
Every trip to the shelf costs time
When the desk is full and you need another book, one has to go back
Question: Which one?





This desk is our model for the whole lecture. The desk is the cache: small and fast. The shelf is the big, slow storage. A trip to the shelf is a cache miss. The question “which book goes back?” is the eviction problem.

Three ways to decide what goes

Random: put back any book
First-In, First-Out (FIFO): put back the book that has been on the desk the longest
Least Recently Used (LRU): put back the book you haven’t touched for the longest time

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
And Random?
Question: Would you clear out your cupboard by throwing out things at random?










Computer scientists call a trip to the shelf a miss, and finding the book on the desk a hit.


In the tutorial, you build this yourself.

Simulation: a desk for three books, 20 different books, 10,000 requests. A book that was used recently is requested again with higher probability, like in real life. Random eviction needs the most trips to the shelf, FIFO fewer, LRU the fewest. Random is not terrible, but it ignores everything we know about what comes next.

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: The perfect strategy needs a crystal ball
text:
The perfect strategy needs a crystal ball

Optimal: Clairvoyance

Keep what you’ll need
Remove what you won’t

Question: What’s the problem?


→ Requires knowledge of the future!

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
LRU in practice

Least Recently Used (LRU) is the dominant strategy
Question: Why is this the better strategy?
Because the recent past predicts the near future
Temporal locality: what you used recently, you will likely need again soon
Books on your desk, apps opened today, people texted this morning
In Belady’s classic comparison, LRU came closest to the crystal ball1

Belady, L. A. (1966). A study of replacement algorithms for a virtual-storage computer. IBM Systems Journal, 5(2), 78–101; see also Christian & Griffiths (2016), ch. 4. In Tutorial III.III you measure LRU against random eviction yourself.

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: The pile on your desk is not a mess
text:
The pile on your desk is not a mess

The economist Yukio Noguchi files everything in one row: whatever he used goes back to the left end
So the most recently used files are always in front
A pile does the same: what you used last lies on top
Proven: searching such a row from the front never takes more than twice as long as the best possible order1






Sleator, D. D. & Tarjan, R. E. (1985). Amortized efficiency of list update and paging rules. Communications of the ACM, 28(2); see also Christian & Griffiths (2016), ch. 4.

text:
Keep it close: caching in logistics
Question: Where do you see this in a warehouse?





Fast movers sit next to the dispatch area, slow movers at the back




A small forward pick area holds what is needed today and is refilled from the large reserve storage: a cache for the warehouse




Regional warehouses keep goods close to the customer









This is spatial locality: keep things where they are used.

Forgetting is a feature

Hermann Ebbinghaus measured how memory fades over time: the forgetting curve
One reading: the brain runs out of space
A better one: the brain keeps close what you will likely need again
What you haven’t used for a long time gets harder to reach, just like LRU1

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: Your attention is a desk for three books
text:
Your attention is a desk for three books

Only a few things fit into your attention at once
Every notification puts a new book on the desk
And pushes another one off
You did not choose which one

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Flooding and poisoning

Flooding: so many notifications that what matters gets pushed out. That is distraction.
Poisoning: false information lands on your desk and you rely on it without checking. That is misinformation.
Both work because attention is small and we trust what is right in front of us.


The terms come from computer security. Cache flooding is a form of Denial-of-Service attack: the system is overloaded with requests, important data is evicted, the system slows down or crashes. Cache poisoning plants false data in a cache, so later requests are answered with wrong content; DNS cache poisoning, for example, sends users to a fake website. Both exploit that a cache is small and is trusted without checking the original source.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Getting it back is expensive

After an interruption, it often takes 20+ minutes to get back on track1
Like a trip to the slowest memory: millions of times more expensive than staying at the desk
Technology and social media are designed to capture attention


Reflection: How many times did you check your phone during this lecture?


Five productivity killers, in cache terms. Overload: too much information at once, the cache capacity is exceeded. Exhaustion: too long without clearing out. Context switching: every interruption of flow costs often 20 minutes or more to get back on track. Distraction: cache flooding by constant notifications and social media. Misinformation: cache poisoning by fake news and misleading information. The result is less creativity, less critical thinking and less productivity.

Order of magnitude from Gloria Mark’s workplace studies, e.g. Mark, G., Gonzalez, V. M., & Harris, J. (2005). No task left behind? Examining the nature of fragmented work. CHI 2005.

title: Lecture III: Caching
section: What gets evicted: first the task, then your goals, then your values
text:
What gets evicted: first the task, then your goals, then your values

Spotlight: what you are doing right now
Starlight: your goals for this year
Daylight: your values, who you want to be1


LRU evicts what you haven’t touched for a long time. If your attention always goes to notifications, you first lose the task, then your goals, and in the end, Williams argues, yourself.


The three levels come from James Williams, a former Google strategist, quoted in Johann Hari’s “Stolen Focus”. Spotlight: immediate goals, your focus, what are you working on right now? Starlight: medium-term goals, your wishes, what matters this year? Daylight: long-term goals, your values, what defines your life direction?

Williams, J. (2018). Stand Out of Our Light. Cambridge University Press; quoted in Hari, J. (2022). Stolen Focus.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
What to do about it

Fewer interruptions: notifications off while you work, one thing at a time
Choose what gets in: be selective with news and feeds
Touch what matters: revisit your goals regularly, so they don’t get evicted


Want to dive deeper? Rolf Dobelli, The Not To-Do List, chapters 15, 46, 51 and 52. Johann Hari, Stolen Focus. And because news is a big source of distraction: Rolf Dobelli, Stop Reading the News.


More tips, in cache terms. Prioritize sleep, nutrition and mindful habits: they maintain cache performance. Take breaks: regular clearing out prevents exhaustion. Time-box your work: structure prevents overflow. Create protected time for deep work and a dedicated workspace: that prevents cache flooding. Meditation and exercise are maintenance routines for the cache. Treat your desk as a cache hierarchy: hot cache on the desk with only today’s tasks, warm cache in a nearby shelf or drawer with this week’s projects, cold storage in the archive or closet for everything else. If you haven’t used it recently, move it away. Distraction can hardly be avoided in today’s world, especially for managers, but it can be reduced, and awareness is the first step.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Self-assessment
Question: Right now:

How many browser tabs do you have open? ___
How many notifications did you receive in the last hour? ___
Check the screen time on your phone.


4 hours a day is 25% of your waking time
That is 3 months of every year
Question: Is that time well invested?


16 waking hours per day. 4 of 16 hours is a quarter, and a quarter of a year is three months of waking time.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
What we covered


The problem: limited space, too much stuff
Every storage system faces the same question: what to keep close and what to clear out.


The solution: keep what you need close, clear out the rest
Fast storage is always small, so we need a rule for clearing out. Least Recently Used works because the recent past predicts the near future.


Your mind is a cache: protecting your attention
Your attention works like a cache: small, valuable and easily flooded, so protect it.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
Why it matters

Your cupboard is full, your desk is cluttered, your inbox overflows. Companies have the same problem: which goods sit next to the loading dock, which files stay on the fast server, which tasks get your attention today.

title: Lecture III: Caching
text:
What you used last, you’ll need next.


Key takeaways, the concepts: caching is universal, it applies to computers, organizations and human cognition. The fundamental trade-off: fast storage is small, large storage is slow. LRU works because of temporal locality, the recent past predicts the near future. Key takeaways for your life: your brain is a cache, with limited capacity, vulnerable to flooding and poisoning. Protect your attention, it is your scarcest and most valuable resource. Apply caching principles to life: keep what you use, remove what you don’t.

What comes to your mind?
Question: What comes to your mind when you think of randomness?

Notes
Answer: Open question. Typical answers are casinos, lotteries, dice and shuffled cards. Let us collect a few, then show that randomness is much more than gambling.
Today we see how randomness helps computers and people: it makes systems fair and secure, it lets us estimate what we cannot calculate, and it helps us search for good solutions to problems that are too big to solve exactly.

Casino

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: What is the opposite of randomness?
text:
What is the opposite of randomness?
Question: What’s the opposite of randomness?


Determinism: same input, same output
Predictability: knowing the outcome in advance
Consistency: reliable patterns



Boredom?


Notes
Answer: Determinism, predictability and consistency. Life without any chance would be reliable, but also a little boring.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
Are these dice fair?
Question: How would you test if dice are fair?


Send them to a lab to check weight and balance
Or simply: roll them many times
Count how often each number comes up
Fair dice show each number about one sixth of the time



Notes
Answer: Roll them many times and count. Fair dice show each number about one sixth of the time; loaded dice show one number far more often. We do not need to look inside the dice, we only need enough rolls.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Fair and loaded dice after 200 rolls
text: Fair and loaded dice after 200 rolls

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Where do you meet randomness every day?
text:
Where do you meet randomness every day?
Question: Where do you encounter randomness in daily life?


A/B tests: visitors are assigned to versions at random
Two-factor codes: random numbers protect your login
Surveys: a random sample gives an unbiased picture
Spotify shuffle: made deliberately less random, because true randomness felt wrong to users1
Tax audits: random checks keep everyone honest
Lotteries: some universities allocate study places by lottery



Notes
Answer: Almost everywhere: online shops test versions at random, login codes are random, surveys and tax audits pick people at random, and some universities allocate study places by lottery. Spotify is the surprise: with true shuffle, the same artist sometimes came twice in a row, and users thought the shuffle was broken.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Randomness is a tool, not just a gamble
text:
Randomness is a tool, not just a gamble


Fairness: nobody can influence the outcome
Security: attackers cannot guess what comes next
Estimating: try many random cases instead of calculating every one
Searching: random steps lead out of dead ends


Estimating and searching are our topics today.

Notes
We use randomness on purpose, not only in games. Fairness: when nobody can influence the outcome, nobody is favored. Security: passwords, keys and login codes are random, so attackers cannot guess the next one. Estimating: instead of calculating every case, we try many random cases and count. Searching: random steps help a search escape dead ends and find better solutions.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
Can a computer roll dice?
Question: How can a machine that only calculates produce randomness?


True randomness

comes from physics
for example radioactive decay or atmospheric noise
cannot be repeated


Pseudo-randomness

comes from a calculation
looks random, but follows a rule
can be repeated exactly



Computers do not roll dice, they calculate. The starting value is called the seed. Same seed, same numbers: that is why your tutorial results are reproducible.

Notes
Answer: It cannot, not really. It calculates numbers that only look random, starting from a seed. For real randomness it needs a physical source, such as noise in its hardware. For simulations, pseudo-randomness is good enough, and the seed makes our results repeatable.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Some things are too big to count
text:
Some things are too big to count
Question: How many possible orders exist for a shuffled deck of cards?

import math
print(math.factorial(52))

80658175170943878571660636856403766975289505440883277824000000000000


That is more than the number of atoms on Earth.2






No computer can ever go through all of these orders one by one.



Question: So how do we answer questions about card games?

Notes
Answer: 52 factorial, about 8 times 10 to the 67. Earth has roughly 10 to the 50 atoms, so there are about a hundred million billion times more orders than atoms. Every well shuffled deck is very likely an order that has never existed before.
Answer: By playing many games and counting. That is the story on the next slide.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
A card game in 1946
Question: Anybody ever heard of Monte Carlo methods?


In 1946, the mathematician Stanislaw Ulam was recovering from an illness and played solitaire
He wondered: what is the chance of winning?
Calculating it was hopeless. So he thought: just play many games and count the wins
The idea became the Monte Carlo method, named after the casino in Monaco3



Notes
Answer: Monte Carlo methods estimate a result by running many random trials and counting the outcomes. Ulam’s question about solitaire is the classic origin story.
Ulam then used the same idea at Los Alamos, together with John von Neumann and Nicholas Metropolis, for nuclear research: chain reactions in nuclear fission were too complex to calculate exactly, so they simulated them with random numbers and counted how often each outcome occurred.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
How could we estimate π?














Throw random points into the square
Count how many land inside the circle
The more points we throw, the closer we get to π



The idea goes back to Buffon, who in 1777 dropped needles on lined paper.4




Notes
Answer: By throwing random points. A circle fits exactly inside the square. The circle covers π/4 of the square, so that is the share of points that land inside it: about 79 %, so about 79 of 100 random points. So: π ≈ 4 × (points inside / all points). Count them, multiply the share by 4, and we have an estimate of π that gets better the more points we throw.
Buffon asked how likely a needle dropped on lined paper crosses a line. The answer contains π, so dropping many needles and counting estimates π. Laplace later pointed out exactly that.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text: Let’s throw points

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Monte Carlo in business: a range instead of a single forecast
text:
Monte Carlo in business: a range instead of a single forecast


Project planning: how likely do we finish before the deadline?
Finance: how much could a portfolio lose in a bad month?
Inventory: how much stock covers an uncertain demand?


The recipe: describe each uncertain input as a range, draw random values, repeat thousands of times, count.

Notes
Instead of a single forecast, Monte Carlo gives a range of outcomes with probabilities. The recipe is always the same: describe each uncertain input by a range or distribution, draw random values for all inputs, compute the result, repeat thousands of times, and look at the distribution of results.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
Will we finish in 25 days?
Three uncertain tasks, most likely 21 days in total, deadline 25 days:











Only 63 % of the simulated projects finish by day 25
Only 18 % finish within the most likely 21 days
On average, the project takes 24 days



Notes
Each task has a minimum, a most likely and a maximum duration: requirements 3, 5 and 10 days, build 8, 12 and 20 days, test 2, 4 and 8 days. Things can go much worse than planned, but rarely much better, so the delays add up. The most likely total of 21 days is the optimistic end of the range, not the middle.

Monte Carlo in real life


You: plan with a buffer. The most likely duration is too optimistic
Companies: plan projects and budgets as a range with probabilities, not as a single number


When you can’t calculate it, simulate it.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Ten cities, one trip: which order is shortest?
text:
Ten cities, one trip: which order is shortest?
Question: In which order would you visit 10 cities by plane with minimal total distance?

import math
print(math.factorial(10))

3628800


Question: What could be a strategy?

Notes
Answer: We cannot see it at a glance: there are 3,628,800 possible orders. Strategies students usually suggest: try all orders, always fly to the nearest city next, or start with any tour and improve it step by step. We look at all three now.
This problem has a name: the travelling salesman problem. We look for the shortest round trip through all cities. It is not the same as the shortest way between two places, which a navigation app finds in a split second.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
Brute force: try every tour

Try every possibility
Total possible tours: 10! = 3,628,800
Guaranteed to find best solution
If each check takes 1ms: 1 hour to check all tours

Question: What could be the problem with this approach?

Notes
Answer: It does not scale. Every additional city multiplies the number of tours, so one hour for ten cities quickly becomes years. The next slide shows how fast.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
What about twenty cities?


For 20 cities: 20! = 2.4 quintillion tours
About 77 million years at 1 ms per check
Every additional city multiplies the effort: hopeless for real problems



Notes
Time complexity grows factorially with the number of cities, and memory requirements increase with the problem size as well. Brute force is not feasible for real-world problems.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Greedy: always take the nearest city
text:
Greedy: always take the nearest city

From each city, fly to the nearest city you have not visited yet
Never look back or change earlier choices
Fast and simple

Problem: the last flights are often very long, because the near cities are already used up.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Hill climbing: improve step by step
text:
Hill climbing: improve step by step

Improve the solution by small changes, keep the better one
Like climbing in fog: you only see your immediate surroundings
You get stuck on a local optimum, a small hill, and never see the mountain

Question: How would you escape a local optimum?

Notes
Answer: Jump somewhere else and climb again, or sometimes accept a step down. Both ideas use chance, and both come next.
Hill climbing iteratively improves a solution by making small changes. Like climbing in fog, it can only see the immediate surroundings and does not know whether higher peaks exist elsewhere. It can get stuck in local optima and gives no guarantee of finding the global optimum.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
section: Shake it up: start again somewhere random
text:
Shake it up: start again somewhere random


When you are stuck, jump to a random new starting point and climb again
Repeat a few times, keep the best result
Computer scientists call this random-restart hill climbing5

title: Lecture V: Randomness

Security: attackers cannot guess what comes next

Searching: random steps lead out of dead ends


Estimating and searching are our topics today.

True randomness

can be repeated exactly

import math

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
A card game in 1946
Question: Anybody ever heard of Monte Carlo methods?

In 1946, the mathematician Stanislaw Ulam was recovering from an illness and played solitaire
He wondered: what is the chance of winning?
Calculating it was hopeless. So he thought: just play many games and count the wins
The idea became the Monte Carlo method, named after the casino in Monaco1


Answer: Monte Carlo methods estimate a result by running many random trials and counting the outcomes. Ulam’s question about solitaire is the classic origin story.
Ulam then used the same idea at Los Alamos, together with John von Neumann and Nicholas Metropolis, for nuclear research: chain reactions in nuclear fission were too complex to calculate exactly, so they simulated them with random numbers and counted how often each outcome occurred.

Christian & Griffiths (2016), ch. 9.

title: Lecture V: Randomness
text:
How could we estimate π?













Throw random points into the square
Count how many land inside the circle
The more points we throw, the closer we get to π


The idea goes back to Buffon, who in 1777 dropped needles on lined paper.1



Answer: By throwing random points. A circle fits exactly inside the square. The circle covers π/4 of the square, so that is the share of points that land inside it: about 79 %, so about 79 of 100 random points. So: π ≈ 4 × (points inside / all points). Count them, multiply the share by 4, and we have an estimate of π that gets better the more points we throw.
Buffon asked how likely a needle dropped on lined paper crosses a line. The answer contains π, so dropping many needles and counting estimates π. Laplace later pointed out exactly that.

Christian & Griffiths (2016), ch. 9.

Monte Carlo in business: a range instead of a single forecast

Project planning: how likely do we finish before the deadline?
Finance: how much could a portfolio lose in a bad month?
Inventory: how much stock covers an uncertain demand?


The recipe: describe each uncertain input as a range, draw random values, repeat thousands of times, count.

Three uncertain tasks, most likely 21 days in total, deadline 25 days:










Only 63 % of the simulated projects finish by day 25
Only 18 % finish within the most likely 21 days

Each task has a minimum, a most likely and a maximum duration: requirements 3, 5 and 10 days, build 8, 12 and 20 days, test 2, 4 and 8 days. Try every possibility
Total possible tours: 10! = 3,628,800

About 77 million years at 1 ms per check

From each city, fly to the nearest city you have not visited yet

Answer: Jump somewhere else and climb again, or sometimes accept a step down. Both ideas use chance, and both come next.

When you are stuck, jump to a random new starting point and climb again

Welcome to this interactive Python tutorial on variables, types, and algorithmic thinking! We’ll explore these concepts through the lens of optimization problems, specifically using the famous “Secretary Problem” as our running example.
The Secretary Problem asks: “If you need to hire the best candidate, and you can only interview candidates one at a time (with no going back), when should you stop and make an offer?” This is a perfect example of optimal stopping and will help us understand how variables and data types play crucial roles in algorithmic thinking. Known academically as the “Optimal Stopping Problem” or “The Marriage Problem”, it asks: If you want to find the best possible partner, and you can only date one person at a time (no going back to previous dates!), when should you stop dating and propose?
Let’s learn how to use Python to make better dating decisions!

text:
Throughout our previous tutorials, we’ve explored fundamental programming concepts through the lens of everyday decision-making. Now, let’s connect these concepts to another important algorithmic idea: caching.

Variables → Like cache entries (storing specific pieces of information)

title: Tutorial III.III: Package Management
text:
Welcome to this guided tutorial on understanding packages and package management in Python! We’ll explore this concept through the lens of library management - how libraries organize, maintain, and share their resources.
Think of Python as your local library’s main building. Just like a library has:

A main collection (Python’s standard library)
Different sections (third-party packages)
A catalog system (a package manager, in our case uv)
Multiple branches (virtual environments / project folders)



Let’s break this down:

Standard Library: Like the core collection every library branch has:

Python comes with essential tools built-in
Data structures (lists, dictionaries, etc.)
Mathematical functions (sin, cos, sqrt, etc.)
Random numbers (random, choice, etc.)

Third-Party Packages: Similar to specialized sections in a library:

Data analysis packages (pandas, numpy) → Research section
Visualization packages (matplotlib, seaborn) → Art books
Web frameworks (Django, Flask) → Technical manuals
Machine learning packages (scikit-learn) → Advanced studies section

Package Manager (uv): Works like the library’s catalog:

Installing packages → Ordering new books
Updating packages → Replacing with newer editions
Uninstalling packages → Removing outdated books
Dependencies → “You must read Book A before Book B”

Project Environments (managed automatically by uv): Like different library branches:

Each branch can have its own collection of books (packages)
Different editions of the same book (package versions)
Specialized sections for different purposes (project-specific dependencies)


The best part? Most Python packages are free to use, thanks to the open-source community!






We use uv in this course for Python version management, virtual environments, and packages. See the separate guide for more details: uv setup.

text:
Coding by hand is not the only way to generate code
Most likely, a lot of you have already used ChatGPT








How do
Large Language
Models work?


Photo by Taylor Vick on Unsplash





Think of them like advanced pattern recognition systems
They have “read” massive amounts of text
Books, websites, articles, code, and more
Text is broken into tokens, parts of words or punctuation
Based on patterns, they can generate new text





Imagine learning a language by reading millions of books
Learns patterns in how words and ideas connect via tokens
Interconnected nodes with weights representing patterns
During training, these weights are adjusted
Once trained, applying them takes much less resources







Using a trained model is called inference.







Not like a search engine!
When asked, it looks for relevant patterns it learned
Like having a huge library in its “memory” to draw from
It can find patterns between concepts and your question
Knows only limited text at once (context window)







Managing context windows is crucial!







After each written token, it predicts “what should come next?”
Like an advanced version of the word prediction on your phone
Picks one of the likely next tokens, not always the most likely one
But can’t actually “think” or “understand” like humans






A setting called temperature controls how much chance is involved
Low temperature: predictable, repetitive answers
High temperature: more creative answers, and more mistakes


The same word as in simulated annealing, and the same idea.

Notes
In simulated annealing from the lecture, a high temperature allows many random moves and a low temperature allows only small, safe ones. In a language model, a higher temperature means that less likely tokens are picked more often.





No true understanding of cause and effect1
Sometimes makes mistakes or “hallucinates”
Mostly only knows what it was trained on2 and can reflect biases
No emotional understanding (but can simulate responses!)3

AI coding assistants

Tools like GitHub Copilot, Cursor or Claude Code work inside your editor
They complete lines and blocks of code and answer questions about your code

Whether you use one, which one and under which license is your own decision.

title: Tutorial V.I: Programming with AI
text:
Used autocomplete before?
When you type on your phone, it suggests the next word.
An AI assistant does the same for code:

You write a comment describing what you want
The AI assistant suggests the code to do it
You accept, modify, or reject the suggestion

It’s autocomplete but much better than what you are used to

title: Tutorial V.I: Programming with AI
text:
Why use an AI assistant?
Benefits you while learning and working with Python:

Faster coding: Less time typing boilerplate code
Learn patterns: See how experienced programmers code
Understand syntax: Get correct syntax without memorizing
Stay in flow: Focus on logic, not syntax errors







Especially helpful when you know WHAT you want to do but forget HOW to do it.

section: What shouldn’t you do with an AI assistant?
text:
What shouldn’t you do with an AI assistant?
Not so good uses of an AI assistant

Replacing learning fundamentals
Accepting code you don’t understand
Skipping practice exercises
Copy-pasting without reading

Always understand what an AI assistant suggests before accepting!
But of course I know you will not do that ;)

title: Tutorial V.I: Programming with AI
text:
Accept without reading?
An AI assistant might suggest code that:

Uses concepts you haven’t learned yet
Contains subtle bugs or misses edge cases
Doesn’t match your requirements
Introduces security risks (an issue in companies, less in this course)

title: Tutorial V.I: Programming with AI
section: My take: Just be careful, ok?
text:
My take: Just be careful, ok?
Your code, your responsibility:

Read the suggestion carefully
Understand what it does
Test it with examples
Modify if needed







Don’t accept code blindly, especially later if things are more complicated.

title: Tutorial V.I: Programming with AI
text:
Key Takeaways

An AI assistant is a tool: You still need to learn fundamentals
Understand before accepting: Read every suggestion carefully
Use it strategically: Syntax help yes, thinking replacement no
Practice: The more you use it, the more helpful it becomes
